flawed_step: Integer capacities imply termination, but do not bound the number of augmentations by the number of edges.
counterexample: Let vertices be s,a,b,t and edges (all directed) be s→a capacity 3, s→b capacity 3, a→b capacity 1, a→t capacity 3, and b→t capacity 3. Thus m=5. Choose augmenting paths in this order: (1) s→a→b→t; (2) s→b→a→t, where b→a is the reverse residual arc of a→b; then repeat this pair twice more. Every augmentation has bottleneck 1. After each odd iteration, the flow on a→b becomes 1; after each even iteration, the reverse arc cancels it back to 0. After six iterations, s→a and s→b each carry 3 and are saturated, so the algorithm terminates. It therefore takes 6 augmenting-path iterations, exceeding m=5.
assessment_summary: A valid sequence of path choices makes Ford–Fulkerson take six iterations on a five-edge integer-capacity network, disproving the claimed universal m-iteration bound.
